name: Dermal rollers / microneedling eyes

card.summary: Needling the thin skin around the eyes, claimed to thicken it and soften circles; microneedling has some evidence for scars, little specific to eyes.
card.note: Non-sterile or non-medical settings have been linked to infection warnings; eye-area skin is delicate.

quick.overview:
Dermal rollers and similar microneedling tools puncture the skin repeatedly with fine needles. Looksmaxxing communities discuss using them around the eyes to thicken thin skin and reduce a tired look.

Microneedling, or collagen induction therapy, has been studied mainly for acne scars, wrinkles and hair loss. Sources reviewed for this entry do not include trials of it specifically for the under-eye or eyelid area.
quick.mechanism: The needles create many tiny punctures, which proponents say trigger the skin's wound-healing response and collagen production. Wikipedia describes the procedure as repeatedly puncturing skin with tiny sterile needles.
quick.risks: Wikipedia notes safety concerns about use in non-medical settings where staff lack infection-control training, citing a 2018 New Mexico health warning and a 2024 CDC announcement of HIV diagnoses in three women after microneedling with platelet-rich plasma at an unlicensed spa. The periorbital skin is delicate and close to the eye.

lead: Microneedling, also called collagen induction therapy, skin needling or dermarolling, is a cosmetic procedure that repeatedly punctures the skin with tiny sterile needles.[1] Handheld rollers and stamping devices are used by clinicians, and rollers are also sold for home use.[1]

In looksmaxxing circles, needling the periorbital skin is discussed as a way to thicken thin under-eye skin and improve its appearance. No trial reviewed for this entry examined microneedling specifically for the eye area.[1]
The best-studied uses of microneedling are acne and other scars, and it has been combined with minoxidil for hair loss in a 2013 pilot study.[1]
infobox: Scars, acne scars, wrinkles, hair loss adjunct[1]

paras: Wikipedia describes microneedling as repeated puncturing of the skin with sterile needles, distinct from microneedles used for transdermal drug delivery. Devices include rollers and stamping tools used by nurses and physicians for scar reduction.[1]

Cited studies on Wikipedia include work on upper-lip wrinkles (Fabbrocini et al., 2012), histological collagen changes combined with platelet-rich plasma (Abuaf et al., 2016), a split-face trial of platelet-rich plasma plus microneedling for atrophic acne scars (Asif, Kanodia and Singh, 2016), and a pilot study of microneedling with minoxidil for hair loss (Dhurat et al., 2013).[1] Efficacy of microneedling combined with platelet-rich plasma, sometimes marketed as a vampire facial, is described as awaiting scientific studies.[1]

Safety concerns focus on non-medical settings without infection control. In September 2018 the New Mexico Department of Health warned that one such business could potentially spread blood-borne infections, and in April 2024 the US CDC announced that three women who had visited the same Albuquerque spa were diagnosed with HIV after vampire facials.[1]
No studies found for the eye area specifically. Studies of microneedling in other areas of the body and face, such as acne scars and wrinkles, exist.[1]
